SOURCE ESSAY:
On the first of May I was sitting outside a café in the Place de la Bastille in Paris staring at the exultant column, crowned with a capering figure, which stands in the place where the people destroyed a prison and ended an age. The thing is a curious example of how symbolic is the great part of human history. As a matter of mere material fact, the Bastille when it was taken was not a horrible prison; it was hardly a prison at all. But it was a symbol, and the people always go by a sure instinct for symbols; for the Chinaman, for instance, at the last General Election, or for President Kruger’s hat in the election before; their poetic sense is perfect. The Chinaman with his pigtail is not an idle flippancy. He does typify with a compact precision exactly the thing the people resent in African policy, the alien and grotesque nature of the power of wealth, the fact that money has no roots, that it is not a natural and familiar power, but a sort of airy and evil magic calling monsters from the ends of the earth. The people hate the mine owner who can bring a Chinaman flying across the sea, exactly as the people hated the wizard who could fetch a flying dragon through the air. It was the same with Mr. Kruger’s hat. His hat (that admirable hat) was not merely a joke. It did symbolise, and symbolise extremely well, the exact thing which our people at that moment regarded with impatience and venom; the old-fashioned, dingy, Republican simplicity, the unbeautiful dignity of the bourgeois, and the heavier truisms of political morality. No; the people are sometimes wrong on the practical side of politics; they are never wrong on the artistic side.

.....

So it was, certainly, with the Bastille. The destruction of the Bastille was not a reform; it was something more important than a reform. It was an iconoclasm; it was the breaking of a stone image. The people saw the building like a giant looking at them with a score of eyes, and they struck at it as at a carved fact. For of all the shapes in which that immense illusion called materialism can terrify the soul, perhaps the most oppressive are big buildings. Man feels like a fly, an accident, in the thing he has himself made. It requires a violent effort of the spirit to remember that man made this confounding thing and man could unmake it. Therefore the mere act of the ragged people in the street taking and destroying a huge public building has a spiritual, a ritual meaning far beyond its immediate political results. It is a religious service. If, for instance, the Socialists were numerous or courageous enough to capture and smash up the Bank of England, you might argue for ever about the inutility of the act, and how it really did not touch the root of the economic problem in the correct manner. But mankind would never forget it. It would change the world.

Architecture is a very good test of the true strength of a society, for the most valuable things in a human state are the irrevocable things—marriage, for instance. And architecture approaches nearer than any other art to being irrevocable, because it is so difficult to get rid of. You can turn a picture with its face to the wall; it would be a nuisance to turn that Roman cathedral with its face to the wall. You can tear a poem to pieces; it is only in moments of very sincere emotion that you tear a town-hall to pieces. A building is akin to dogma; it is insolent, like a dogma. Whether or no it is permanent, it claims permanence like a dogma. People ask why we have no typical architecture of the modern world, like impressionism in painting. Surely it is obviously because we have not enough dogmas; we cannot bear to see anything in the sky that is solid and enduring, anything in the sky that does not change like the clouds of the sky. But along with this decision which is involved in creating a building, there goes a quite similar decision in the more delightful task of smashing one. The two of necessity go together. In few places have so many fine public buildings been set up as here in Paris, and in few places have so many been destroyed. When people have finally got into the horrible habit of preserving buildings, they have got out of the habit of building them. And in London one mingles, as it were, one’s tears because so few are pulled down.

.....

As I sat staring at the column of the Bastille, inscribed to Liberty and Glory, there came out of one corner of the square (which, like so many such squares, was at once crowded and quiet) a sudden and silent line of horsemen. Their dress was of a dull blue, plain and prosaic enough, but the sun set on fire the brass and steel of their helmets; and their helmets were carved like the helmets of the Romans. I had seen them by twos and threes often enough before. I had seen plenty of them in pictures toiling through the snows of Friedland or roaring round the squares at Waterloo. But now they came file after file, like an invasion, and something in their numbers, or in the evening light that lit up their faces and their crests, or something in the reverie into which they broke, made me inclined to spring to my feet and cry out, “The French soldiers!” There were the little men with the brown faces that had so often ridden through the capitals of Europe as coolly as they now rode through their own. And when I looked across the square I saw that the two other corners were choked with blue and red; held by little groups of infantry. The city was garrisoned as against a revolution.

Of course, I had heard all about the strike, chiefly from a baker. He said he was not going to “Chomer.” I said, “Qu’est-ce que c’est que le chome?” He said, “Ils ne veulent pas travailler.” I said, “Ni moi non plus,” and he thought I was a class-conscious collectivist proletarian. The whole thing was curious, and the true moral of it one not easy for us, as a nation, to grasp, because our own faults are so deeply and dangerously in the other direction. To me, as an Englishman (personally steeped in the English optimism and the English dislike of severity), the whole thing seemed a fuss about nothing. It looked like turning out one of the best armies in Europe against ordinary people walking about the street. The cavalry charged us once or twice, more or less harmlessly. But, of course, it is hard to say how far in such criticisms one is assuming the French populace to be (what it is not) as docile as the English. But the deeper truth of the matter tingled, so to speak, through the whole noisy night. This people has a natural faculty for feeling itself on the eve of something—of the Bartholomew or the Revolution or the Commune or the Day of Judgment. It is this sense of crisis that makes France eternally young. It is perpetually pulling down and building up, as it pulled down the prison and put up the column in the Place de La Bastille. France has always been at the point of dissolution. She has found the only method of immortality. She dies daily.

message.content:
On May first, I found myself seated at an outdoor café in Paris's Place de la Bastille, gazing at the triumphant column adorned with a lively figure that marks the site where a prison was demolished, signaling the end of an era. This monument serves as an intriguing illustration of how much of human history is steeped in symbolism. In practical terms, the Bastille was not a grim fortress when it was stormed; it could hardly be termed a prison at all. However, it stood as a potent symbol, and people possess an innate ability to grasp such symbols—much like how the Chinese figure influenced the last General Election, or how President Kruger’s distinctive hat resonated in the election prior. These symbols are not mere whims; they encapsulate precisely what the populace resents, whether it be the alienating power of wealth or the outdated, mundane dignity of the bourgeois. The aversion to the mine owner who could summon a Chinese worker from afar mirrors the historical disdain for the sorcerer who could conjure dragons. Similarly, Mr. Kruger’s hat transcended mere humor; it effectively represented the impatience and frustration that our society felt toward the dullness of traditional Republican values and the burdensome truths of political ethics. While the public may sometimes err in practical political matters, their artistic instincts remain unfailingly accurate.

This phenomenon was undoubtedly applicable to the Bastille. The act of its destruction was not merely a reform; it represented something far more significant—an iconoclastic moment that shattered a stone idol. The crowds perceived the building as a colossal entity staring down at them with myriad eyes, prompting them to strike at it as if it were a tangible representation of their collective frustration. Among the myriad forms that materialism can assume to oppress the human spirit, few are as stifling as grand structures. In such moments, a person may feel utterly insignificant, akin to a fly caught in a web of their own creation. It takes a considerable mental effort to recall that humans constructed these imposing edifices and, thus, possess the power to dismantle them. Consequently, the act of the ragged masses seizing and demolishing a monumental public structure carries a profound spiritual and ritualistic significance that transcends its immediate political implications. If, for instance, a sizable and daring group of Socialists were to seize and destroy the Bank of England, debates over the act's practicality could ensue indefinitely, yet humanity would never forget it. Such an event would leave an indelible mark on the world.

Architecture serves as a compelling gauge of a society's true strength, particularly because the most valuable aspects of a civilization are often those that cannot be undone—marriage, for example. Architecture, due to its inherent difficulty in being dismantled, approaches a level of permanence unmatched by other art forms. One can easily turn a painting away from view, but how cumbersome it would be to rotate a Roman cathedral to conceal it. A poem can be ripped apart, but only in moments of intense emotion do we resort to destroying a town hall. Structures demand a commitment akin to dogma; they assert their permanence with the same authority as a religious doctrine. People often wonder why typical modern architecture does not exist, akin to the impressionist movement in painting. The answer is clear: we lack enough dogmas to sustain such creations. We cannot bear to witness anything solid and enduring in our cultural sky, preferring instead the transient forms of clouds. Yet, the act of creating a building is intrinsically tied to the equally significant act of destroying one. These two actions are bound together in a dance of societal evolution. In Paris, a city celebrated for its magnificent public buildings, one also finds a history of destruction. When a society becomes overly focused on preserving its structures, it may lose the ability to create new ones. In London, this duality is palpable; one often mingles sorrow with the realization that so few buildings have been demolished.

As I continued to contemplate the column of the Bastille, inscribed with the words "Liberty" and "Glory," a sudden procession of horsemen emerged from a corner of the square, which, like many such places, was both bustling and serene. Clad in dull blue uniforms that were rather uninspiring, the sunlight ignited the brass and steel of their helmets, which were reminiscent of Roman designs. I had encountered these soldiers in the past, often depicted in images from the snowy battlegrounds of Friedland or galloping through the squares of Waterloo. But this time, they advanced in a long, unbroken line, and something about their sheer numbers, along with the evening light illuminating their faces and crests, stirred me to the point where I felt an impulse to leap up and exclaim, “The French soldiers!” There they were—the small men with brown faces who had so casually traversed the capitals of Europe now rode through their own streets with equal ease. Surveying the square further, I noticed that the other corners were crowded with blue and red-clad infantry, establishing a sense of order as if to guard against an uprising.

I had heard whispers of the ongoing strike, primarily from a local baker. He mentioned he would not be participating in “Chomer.” Curious, I asked, “What is this ‘chome’?” He explained, “Ils ne veulent pas travailler.” I replied, “Neither do I,” which led him to assume I was a class-conscious member of the proletariat. The entire situation was perplexing and revealed a moral lesson that remains challenging for us as a nation to fully comprehend, particularly given our own tendencies that veer dangerously in the opposite direction. As an Englishman, steeped in a culture of optimism and a tendency to shy away from severity, this whole affair appeared to be an overreaction. It felt like deploying one of the continent's finest armies against ordinary citizens merely strolling through the streets. The cavalry charged us occasionally, but with little consequence. Nevertheless, it is difficult to ascertain how much of such criticism relies on the presumption that the French populace behaves as docilely as the English, which it does not. However, beneath the surface noise of that chaotic night, a deeper truth reverberated. This society possesses a remarkable ability to sense that it stands on the brink of something monumental—be it the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre, the Revolution, the Commune, or even the Day of Judgment. This acute perception of crisis is what keeps France eternally youthful. It is a nation in a perpetual cycle of destruction and creation, as evidenced by the dismantling of the Bastille and the erection of the column in its place. France has discovered its unique form of immortality; it undergoes daily deaths and rebirths.
